claims.text: The starting composite contains tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite develops phase separation during processing and service.
The untreated W–Cu composite develops interfacial voids during processing and service.
A nanoscale graded refractory carbide/nitride layer is to be deposited on tungsten surfaces before consolidation.
The proposed coating will suppress diffusion-driven phase separation in W–Cu.
The proposed coating will reduce interfacial void formation.
The coating acts as a diffusion barrier between W and Cu during high-temperature processing and irradiation.
An engineered particle coating can promote interfacial adhesion.
The proposed coating modifies interfacial energy.
Improved interfacial bonding and carbide formation can reduce cracks or micro-holes at a coated composite interface.
The graded structure of the proposed carbide/nitride coating enhances adhesion at the W–Cu interface.
Reducing interfacial voids and phase separation will maintain or improve the composite's thermal conductivity.
The coated W–Cu composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity than an untreated composite under equivalent high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
Interfacial diffusion or reaction-layer development during joining depends on processing temperature and time.
High thermal flux and irradiation are relevant considerations for interfaces between tungsten-based plasma-facing materials and copper-based cooling components.
The intervention will remain effective across typical industrial consolidation temperatures and plasma-facing joint heat-flux and irradiation exposures.
Long-term stability of the nanoscale coating under prolonged irradiation and thermal cycling is not established.
